readerTitle: The scariest risk is rarely the biggest one
caseNote: 가상 사례 두 개 (급여 대행 회사, 배관 회사) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 위험은 느낌이 아니라 '일어날 확률 × 일어났을 때의 피해'로 같은 저울에 올려 비교한다. 다만 살아남을 수 없는 피해는 곱셈과 별도로 다룬다.
misconception: 가장 무서운 위험이나 가장 자주 귀찮게 하는 위험이 가장 큰 위험이다.

sources.text: 위험관리의 표준 개념 (기대손실 = 발생 확률 × 영향, 위험 매트릭스)

factChecks.note: 적용 문제: A 체크리스트·교육 $3,000, 재방문 절반 → 절감 $5,000. B 보너스 $4,000, 퇴사 확률 20%→10% → 절감 $3,000. C 보험 해지 절약 $1,200, 그러나 $100,000 청구 시 회사 존립 위험. 특정 국가의 보험 의무 여부는 다루지 않음.

cards.title: The scariest risk is rarely the biggest one
body: Dana runs a 12-person payroll firm. She loses sleep over a data breach. Marco runs a plumbing company with six vans. What bugs him most is the van that keeps breaking down.
Both are watching the wrong risk. Their fears aren't silly. They're just sizing risks by feel.

image.label: Two business owners, each with a worry cloud over their head
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눠 왼쪽은 사무실의 급여 대행 회사 대표(머리 위 구름에 자물쇠 아이콘), 오른쪽은 작업복 차림의 배관 회사 대표(구름에 고장 난 밴). 따뜻한 플랫 일러스트. 실제 로고·상표 없음.

cards.title: You can fix one risk this quarter.
body: You're Dana. Your payroll firm has time and budget to tackle one risk properly. Your rough estimates for the coming year:
Data breach: 1% chance, $300,000 if it happens. Payroll delayed by a system glitch: about 6 times a year, $1,500 in credits each time. Your biggest client leaves: 20% chance, $60,000 in lost profit.

options.text: The data breach. It's the one that could ruin you
options.feedback: Right that it can't be ignored, but its expected yearly cost is the smallest here. A rare disaster is often better handled by insurance than by your whole quarter.

options.text: The payroll delays. They happen all the time
options.feedback: Frequent problems feel urgent because you see them. But each hit is small, so the yearly total isn't the largest.
It's neither the scariest nor the noisiest, but chance times cost makes it the biggest. Next card shows the math.

cards.title: Multiply, then compare.
body: The scariest risk came last. The most annoying one came second. The quiet one Dana barely thought about came first.

cards.title: Probability times impact
body: Every risk has two sizes: **how likely** it is, and **how much it hurts** when it happens. Multiply them and you get its *expected cost*, what it costs you on average per year.
This puts very different risks on one scale. A rare disaster and a weekly annoyance can finally be compared side by side.

image.label: A grid with likelihood on one axis and impact on the other
image.brief: 위험 매트릭스 인포그래픽. 가로축 "How likely", 세로축 "How much it hurts". 오른쪽 위 칸이 진한 색. 점 세 개: "Breach"(왼쪽 위), "Delays"(오른쪽 아래), "Client leaves"(가운데 위쪽, 가장 큰 점).

cards.softwareNote: In a software business, the same math compares a rare full outage with a small bug that hits some users every week. The weekly bug often costs more over a year, even though the outage gets the post-mortem.

cards.title: For Marco, the boring risk wins.
body: Marco runs the same math on his plumbing company. Here the top risk is the frequent, small one: jobs his team has to go back and redo for free.
Gut feel picked the scary risk for Dana and the noisy one for Marco. The multiplication picked differently in each business.

cards.title: Rough numbers are enough.
body: You won't know the real odds. That's fine. The goal is ranking, not precision. Even "about 1 in 5" and "roughly $50,000" will sort a list better than a hunch.

Then compare each fix with what it saves. A $4,000 backup system that cuts Dana's delays from six a year to two saves **$6,000** in expected cost. That's worth doing. A fix that costs more than it saves usually isn't.

cards.title: Averages hide the risks that end you.
body: Dana's breach has a small expected cost: $3,000. But if it happens, $300,000 could close a 12-person firm. You don't live the average. You live the one year it happens.
So use the multiplication to rank everyday risks. For anything you couldn't survive, look at **impact alone** and cap it with insurance, limits or by avoiding it.
Also be humble about rare events. A 1% guess is often just a guess.

cards.title: Marco has $5,000 to spend on risk.
body: Using his numbers from the chart, which move is best?

options.text: A $3,000 job checklist and training that halves callbacks
options.feedback: It saves about $5,000 a year for $3,000. It targets the biggest expected cost and pays for itself.

options.text: A $4,000 retention bonus that halves the chance his lead tech quits
options.feedback: It saves about $3,000 in expected cost for $4,000. It may still help morale, but on risk alone it costs more than it saves.

options.text: Drop water-damage insurance to save $1,200, since the expected cost is only $2,000
options.feedback: The average looks small, but one $100,000 claim could sink the company. This is the kind of risk to judge by impact alone.

cards.title: Size every risk twice: how likely, and how bad.
body: Multiply the two to rank your risks on one scale. Then handle the ones you couldn't survive separately, however rare they seem.
**Try it today:** list your top five risks. Next to each, write a rough chance per year and a rough cost. Multiply. Is the top of the list the one you worry about most?
